## Data structures in R

### Vector: the foundational R data structure

#### Numeric

Example 1:

```{r}
x <- c(0.5, 0.6)
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)
summary(age)
```

Example 2:

```{r}
age <- c(35, 24, 18, 24)
mean(age)
```

#### Logical

```{r}
x <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
x <- c(T, F)
```

#### Character

```{r}
x <- c("a", "b", "c")
class <- c("M", "F", "F", "M")
```

#### Integer

```{r}
x <- 9:29
```

#### Complex

```{r}
x <- c(1 + 0i, 2 + 4i)
```

### Matrix and matrix operations

```{r}
(x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3))
x
(y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2))
x %*% y
```

### List

```{r}
(x <- list(1, "a", TRUE, 1 + 4i))
x
```

### Factor

```{r}
x <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"))
```

### Missing values

Create a vector with NAs:

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)
```

Return a logical vector indicating which elements are NA:

```{r}
is.na(x)
```

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 4, "NA", 5)
bad <- is.na(x)
print(bad)
x[!bad]
```

What if there are multiple R objects and you want to take the subset with no missing values in any of those objects?

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, 5)
y <- c("a", "b", NA, "d", NA, "f")
good <- complete.cases(x, y)
good
```

## Coercion

If a character is present in a vector, R converts everything in the vector to character strings.

If a vector contains only logical values and numbers, R converts the logical values to numbers; every `TRUE` becomes `1`, and every `FALSE` becomes `0`.

```{r}
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))
```

## Create data

Data frames are more general than matrices because a data frame can contain different data types (numeric, character, etc.), similar to what you can see in SPSS or SAS.

### Let’s create a data frame

```{r}
studentID <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
math_score <- c(12, 17, 10, 9, NA)
gender <- c("M", "F", "M", "M", "F")
it_score <- c(13, 18, 11, 10, 19)
scoredata <- data.frame(studentID, gender, math_score, it_score)
scoredata
```

### Create data from keyboard

Steps:

1. Create a data frame (or matrix) with variable names.
2. Invoke the text editor on the created object.

```{r}
data_class2 <- data.frame(height = numeric(0), weight = numeric(0), bmi = numeric(0))
# data_class2 <- edit(data_class2)
```

## Data importation

R can import data from different sources, such as:

- Text files (ASCII, XML, web scraping)
- Spreadsheets
- Statistical packages (SAS, SPSS, Stata)
- Database management systems (SQL, MySQL, Oracle, Access)

### Homework: import data from a statistical package and from a database management system

```{r}
data_class <- read.table("datasets/class_data.txt", header = TRUE)
variable.names(data_class)
head(data_class)
tail(data_class)
data_class[10:20, ]
summary(data_class$WEIGHT)
length(data_class$WEIGHT)
data_class[, -1]
data_class$WEIGHT
```

### Using built-in datasets in R

```{r}
data() # list of datasets currently available
data("airquality")
variable.names(airquality)
str(airquality)
```

## Exploratory data analysis

Examine numerical variables using common summaries:

```{r}
data_class
summary(data_class)
str(data_class)
```

### Summary statistics

```{r}
summary(data_class)
apply(data_class, 1, mean)
apply(data_class, 2, sd)
c(mean(data_class$HEIGHT), sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
c(mean(data_class$WEIGHT), sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
c(Mean = mean(data_class$HEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
c(Mean = mean(data_class$WEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
```

## Variation and covariation using both numerical and graphical methods

### Relationship between a categorical and a continuous variable

```{r}
data("iris")
head(iris)
mean(iris$Petal.Length)
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "virginica"])
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
```

Visualize differences in continuous variables between categories using a box-and-whisker plot:

```{r}
boxplot(iris$Sepal.Length ~ iris$Species,
    data = iris,
    main = "Comparison of categorical vs quantitative"
)
```

### Relationship between two categorical variables

```{r}
ucba <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucba)

cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba)
(cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba))
prop.table(cross, 1)
```

## Simpson’s paradox

This is a phenomenon where a trend that appears in combined groups disappears or reverses when the data are broken down into groups.

```{r}
cross2 <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba[ucba$Dept == "F", ])
prop.table(cross2, 1)
```

## Graphical summaries

### Bar chart

```{r}
dat <- read.table(text = "ProdA ProdB ProdC ProdD
1 110 50 60 70
2 120 50 80 65", header = TRUE)

barplot(as.matrix(dat), beside = TRUE, col = c("Red", "green"))
```

```{r}
dat <- read.table(text = "A   B   C   D   E   F    G
1 10 80 30 90 70 60  90
2 20 50 70 50 40 10  40
3 60 80 80 60 60 30 160
4 20 40 70 80 20 10  70", header = TRUE)

barplot(as.matrix(dat))
```

### Scatter plot

```{r}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
plot(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
plot(data_class[, 1], data_class[, 2], main = "Graph")
cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
```

## Linear models

```{r}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)$coefficient)

data_lm <- lm(HEIGHT ~ WEIGHT, data = data_class)
summary(data_lm)
plot(data_lm)
hist(data_class$HEIGHT)
hist(data_class$WEIGHT, col = "blue")
```

A linear model with a smooth line:

```{r}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)$coefficient)
lines(lowess(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT), col = "blue")
cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
```

## Data management

Create another variable:

```{r}
attach(data_class)
(BMI <- WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2)
(BMI <- round(WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2, digit = 2))
head(cbind(data_class, BMI), n = 5)
new_data_class <- cbind(data_class, BMI)
tail(cbind(data_class, BMI), n = 10)
summary(BMI)
stem(BMI, scale = 2)
```

## Dates

```{r}
today <- Sys.Date()
format(today, format = "%B %d %Y")
format(today, format = "%A")
```

```{r}
today <- Sys.Date()
dob <- as.Date("1982-02-10")
# today <- as.Date("2024-08-25")
difftime(today, dob, units = "days")

startdate <- as.Date("2004-02-13")
enddate <- as.Date("2011-01-22")
days <- enddate - startdate
days
```

## Subsetting

Use `$`, `[ ]`, or `[[ ]]` to subset data. For example:

```{r}
manager <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
country <- c("US", "US", "UK", "UK", "UK")
gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F")
age <- c(32, 45, 25, 39, 99)
q1 <- c(5, 3, 3, 3, 2)
q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2)
q3 <- c(5, 2, 5, 4, 1)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 5, NA, 2)
q5 <- c(5, 5, 2, NA, 1)
leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age, q1, q2, q3, q4, q5,
    stringsAsFactors = TRUE
)
leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age, q1, q2, q3, q4, q5)
str(leadership)
names(leadership)
```

What you can do:

- combine the scores of the five questions
- handle missing values
- create a dataset of the variables you want
- create age groups
- note that `99` indicates a missing value

### Missing value handling

```{r}
leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA
leadership

leadership$agecat[leadership$age > 75] <- "Elder"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75] <- "Middle Aged"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age < 35] <- "Young"
```

Listwise deletion is one of several methods of handling incomplete datasets. You may also replace missing values by the mean of the remaining data.

```{r}
is.na(leadership[, 5:9])
newdata <- na.omit(leadership)
newdata
```

### Sorting data

```{r}
order(leadership$age)
newdata2 <- leadership[order(leadership$age), ]
```

### Merging data sets

To merge two data frames horizontally, use `merge()`. In most cases, two data frames are joined by one or more common key variables.

To join two datasets vertically, use `rbind()`; note that the two data sets must have the same variables.

### Selecting variables and observations

```{r}
newdata3 <- leadership[, c(5:9)]
myvars <- c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")
(newdata3 <- leadership[myvars])

newdata4 <- leadership[, c(-1, -2)]
(newdata4 <- leadership[, -(1:5)])

newdata5 <- leadership[, c(-1, -7)]
leadership[[4]]
leadership$age
newdata6 <- leadership[c(-1, -3), ]
newdata6 <- leadership[c(2, 4, 5), ]
newdata7 <- subset(leadership, age >= 35 | age < 24, select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5))
```

```{r}
attach(leadership)
(newdata7 <- leadership[gender == "M" & age > 30, ])
detach(leadership)
```
